Hyperparameter Tuning with Bayesian Optimization

Source: vignettes/bayesian-optimization-tuning.Rmd
bayesian-optimization-tuning.Rmd

Introduction

The companion vignette Bayesian Optimization with TabPFN shows the mechanics of the optimizer on a known analytic function. This vignette takes the same machinery to a realistic task: tuning the hyperparameters of a model when every evaluation means a full cross-validation run.

We tune a k-nearest-neighbours regressor on mtcars by choosing the number of neighbours k and the distance-weighting exponent power. The objective is noisy, non-convex, and cheap enough to run in seconds — a good stand-in for the kind of expensive black box Bayesian optimization is built for.

Requires the full tabpfn package (>= 8.1.0) and tabpfn-extensions[bayesian_optimization]. Install with setup_tabpfn(install_bayesian_optimization = TRUE).

The black-box objective

Each evaluation runs 5-fold cross-validation of a weighted k-NN and returns the out-of-fold RMSE. Lower is better, so we will minimize:

knn_cv_rmse <- function(k, power, folds = 5, seed = 7) {
  set.seed(seed)
  X <- as.matrix(mtcars[, c("cyl", "disp", "hp", "wt", "qsec")])
  y <- mtcars$mpg
  n <- nrow(X)

  fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(folds), length.out = n))
  d <- as.matrix(stats::dist(X))
  errs <- numeric(n)

  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    tr  <- fold != fold[i]                 # training = all folds except i's
    dd  <- d[i, tr]
    ord <- order(dd)[seq_len(k)]
    w   <- 1 / (dd[ord] + 1e-8)^power
    pred <- sum(w * y[tr][ord]) / sum(w)
    errs[i] <- pred - y[i]
  }

  sqrt(mean(errs^2))
}

# Wrapper the optimizer calls: `par` is a named vector c(k = , power = ).
objective <- function(par) {
  k <- max(1L, min(15L, round(par[["k"]])))   # k is discrete -> round it
  knn_cv_rmse(k, par[["power"]])
}

A quick look at the landscape confirms it is not something a grid search nails easily — there is a sharp ridge as power grows:

grid <- expand.grid(k = 1:15, power = seq(0, 3, length.out = 40))
grid$rmse <- mapply(function(k, p) knn_cv_rmse(k, p), grid$k, grid$power)

Running TabPFN Bayesian optimization

We search k in [1, 15] and power in [0, 3], with 6 random initial points followed by 14 acquisition steps (20 evaluations total):

bo <- tryCatch(
  if (run_live) {
    tab_pfn_bayesian_optimization(
      fun      = objective,
      bounds   = list(k = c(1, 15), power = c(0, 3)),
      n_init   = 6,
      n_iter   = 14,
      maximize = FALSE,      # minimize RMSE
      device   = "auto",
      random_state = 1,
      verbose  = FALSE
    )
  } else {
    NULL
  },
  error = function(e) NULL
)

used_live <- !is.null(bo)
if (!used_live) bo <- bo_trace

data.frame(
  source   = if (used_live) "live TabPFN run" else "precomputed trace",
  k        = round(bo$best_x[["k"]]),
  power    = round(bo$best_x[["power"]], 2),
  cv_rmse  = round(bo$best_y, 4)
)
##            source  k power cv_rmse
## 1 live TabPFN run 12  1.88  2.1585

How does it compare with random search?

Bayesian optimization earns its keep by beating a naive baseline on the same budget. Let’s spend 20 evaluations on random search and compare the best value found so far:

set.seed(42)
n_budget <- nrow(bo$X)                       # match the BO budget exactly
rs_k     <- round(runif(n_budget, 1, 15))
rs_power <- runif(n_budget, 0, 3)
rs_y     <- mapply(function(k, p) objective(c(k = k, power = p)), rs_k, rs_power)
library(ggplot2)

hist_df <- rbind(
  data.frame(eval = seq_along(bo$y), best = cummin(bo$y), method = "TabPFN BO"),
  data.frame(eval = seq_along(rs_y), best = cummin(rs_y), method = "Random search")
)

ggplot(hist_df, aes(eval, best, colour = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Best CV RMSE so far",
       x = "Objective evaluation", y = "Best RMSE") +
  theme_minimal()

Where did the optimizer look?

Plotting the objective surface together with the points TabPFN BO evaluated shows how it concentrates around the good region instead of sampling blindly:

pts <- data.frame(
  k = bo$X[, 1],
  power = bo$X[, 2],
  type = c(rep("initial", 6), rep("acquisition", nrow(bo$X) - 6))
)

ggplot(grid, aes(k, power)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = rmse)) +
  geom_point(data = pts, aes(shape = type), colour = "white", size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#2c7fb8", high = "#deebf7") +
  labs(title = "CV RMSE surface and BO evaluations",
       fill = "RMSE", shape = "Point") +
  theme_minimal()

Warm-starting from earlier runs

If you already evaluated some configurations — a pilot study, a previous session, or a parallel worker — feed them straight in with init_X / init_y and let BO continue from there. Here we resume the first run and add 10 more iterations:

bo2 <- tryCatch(
  if (run_live) {
    tab_pfn_bayesian_optimization(
      fun      = objective,
      bounds   = list(k = c(1, 15), power = c(0, 3)),
      init_X   = bo$X,
      init_y   = bo$y,
      n_iter   = 10,
      maximize = FALSE,
      device   = "auto",
      random_state = 2,
      verbose  = FALSE
    )
  } else {
    NULL
  },
  error = function(e) NULL
)

best_warm <- if (is.null(bo2)) bo_trace$bo2_best_y else bo2$best_y

data.frame(
  run        = c("first run (20 evals)", "warm start (+10 evals)"),
  best_rmse  = round(c(bo$best_y, best_warm), 4)
)
##                      run best_rmse
## 1   first run (20 evals)    2.1585
## 2 warm start (+10 evals)    2.1448

Warm-starting reuses every past evaluation, so the second run never regresses below the first run’s best value.

Notes

  • The search domain is always the unit hypercube internally; bounds are scaled in and out automatically, and fun is always called in the original space.
  • EI maximizes: pass maximize = FALSE to minimize, as we did for RMSE.
  • Discrete hyperparameters (like k) are handled by rounding inside the objective. Keep the bounds continuous for the optimizer and let your wrapper snap to valid values.
  • Increase n_estimators for a more stable surrogate at the cost of speed, and use device = "auto" to pick up a GPU when one is available.
  • To drive the loop yourself — batch candidates, asynchronous workers, custom stopping rules — use tab_pfn_bo_suggest().
  • When the Bayesian optimization extension is not configured, the figures above reuse a precomputed optimization trace (inst/extdata/bo_tuning_trace.rds) instead of running the surrogate live.
